lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Find and sketch three right angles and three non-right angles in the room. Label each.

FEEDBACK
Labels must match the tester, not just the sketch beauty.

WATCH FOR
Photographing without classifying leaves the hunt incomplete.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Complete an angle hunt of at least twelve finds. Tally right / smaller / larger. Write two sentences about where right angles were most common.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example log: desk corner — right; open laptop — larger than right; pizza slice tip — smaller than right.

TRY FIRST
Find and sketch three right angles and three non-right angles in the room. Label each.

FEEDBACK
Labels must match the tester, not just the sketch beauty.
teach_steps.explain:
Angles appear in the environment: book corners, window frames, clock hands, open doors. An angle hunt records and classifies them.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Photographing without classifying leaves the hunt incomplete. Correct the value or method, not just the appearance of the digits.
